stops.name: The Mount of Olives, the cell, brother Pelagius
stops.campa: On the Mount of Olives, within sight of the garden another story in this atlas keeps its own vigil, Pelagia builds herself a narrow cell and takes up the life of a solitary monk under the name Pelagius, known to the brothers of the mountain only as a beardless eunuch of unusual holiness, fasting hard, speaking little, admitting no one. Pilgrims climb to be blessed by the famous eunuch monk of Olivet without guessing what the Legend already knows: that the pearl of Antioch and the anchorite of the Mount are the same flesh, the same water, differently dressed.

stops.name: The Mount of Olives, the death of brother Pelagius, and the truth
stops.campa: Years into the solitary life, brother Pelagius dies in the cell on Olivet, and the brothers who come to wash the body for burial find not the eunuch monk they have known for a decade but a woman, wasted by fasting to nothing, no trace left of the silks or the litter of Antioch. Word runs back down the mountain to Jerusalem and further, to the city she fled, where those who remember the actress called Margaret learn only now, at the graveside, which of her names was true. The church fixes her memory on the eighth of October, the date this cell finally tells its secret.

stops.name: Antioch, the wedding night, the midnight flight
stops.campa: In the version the Golden Legend keeps folded inside its own chapter on Pelagia, a bride called by two names, Margaret and Pelagia both, the record insisting on the doubling rather than resolving it, is married in the customary way and lies down in her husband's house. That night she does not go to him. At midnight she rises, commits herself to God alone, cuts off her hair with her own hand, and dresses herself in a man's habit taken from she does not say where, and is gone before her husband wakes to find the bed half-empty and the door unbarred.
stops.quote: Margaret had twin names; she was called Margaret and Pelagia... and that night she kept from the company of her husband. At midnight, she committed herself to God, cut off her hair, and clad herself in the habit of a man.
stops.quote_source: Golden Legend, Life of St. Pelagia (as carried in essays/215_runaway_bride.md)

stops.name: Antioch, the monastery gate, 'brother Pelagia'
stops.campa: She flees not to the desert alone but to a monastery of monks, and asks entrance in her cut hair and borrowed habit; the brothers, deceived exactly as she means them to be, take her in and call her brother Pelagia: the masculine title laid directly over the feminine name, a contradiction the Legend records without comment, as though it were the whole point. She lives out her life among them undiscovered, one more runaway bride keeping the same trick that saved Thecla and will save Marina after her: the habit changes what men see; the name, half-changed, is where the truth still hides.
stops.quote: Then she fled to a monastery of monks, who called her brother Pelagia.
stops.quote_source: Golden Legend, Life of St. Pelagia (as carried in essays/215_runaway_bride.md)

stops.name: Al-Qalamoun, near Tripoli: a father resolves to raise his daughter as a monk
stops.campa: Two hundred years later and eastward down the same coast, in a village near Tripoli in Lebanon, a Christian merchant named Eugenius loses his wife and is left with an infant daughter, Marina. Nearing old age he resolves to give away his goods and enter the monastery of Qannoubine in the mountains above, and grieves that he must first place the child in a convent of women, apart from him. Marina, still young, will not hear of the separation: let her go with him as a boy, she says, and be raised a monk at his side rather than a stranger in a house of strangers.

stops.name: Qannoubine, the Kadisha Valley, the monk Marinos
stops.campa: Eugenius shaves his daughter's head, dresses her as a boy, and brings her to Qannoubine in the cliffside valley the Syriac tongue calls Kadisha, the holy valley, where they take their vows together and share a cell as father and son. She is known now as the monk Marinos, and grows into the discipline so entirely, in the fasts, the silence, the labor of hauling the monastery's grain to and from the town below by mule, that no brother in twenty years suspects the body under the habit is a woman's, not even the abbot who will one day condemn her unheard.

stops.name: Qannoubine, the false accusation, the child raised at the gate
stops.campa: Sent down with the mule to fetch supplies, Marinos lodges at an inn whose keeper's daughter is got with child by a soldier; to save herself she names the young monk as the father. The innkeeper storms to the monastery; Marinos, given the choice between confessing falsely or exposing her own sex to clear her name, kneels and confesses to a sin she has not committed, choosing shame as a man over the truth as a woman. She is driven from the gate, and when the child is born it is given to her, the disgraced monk, to raise alone outside the walls for ten years on borrowed milk.

stops.name: Qannoubine, the death of Marinos, and the truth at the grave
stops.campa: Marinos dies still uncleared, still confessed to a sin never hers, and the brothers who come to wash the body for burial find, as on the Mount of Olives, a woman where they expected a man: the same discovery, the same grief for having doubted, a mountain valley answering a mountain garden a world away. The abbot and monks fall on their knees before the body begging forgiveness of the saint they condemned unheard, and the innkeeper who accused her repents at the news. The child she raised on borrowed milk becomes a monk of the same house, keeping in silence the second half of a lie that was never hers to begin with.

stops.name: Domrémy, her father's garden
stops.campa: In the garden behind Jacques d'Arc's house at Domrémy a summer voice comes to a girl of thirteen, and behind the first voice, Michael's, come two more, crowned in rich and precious crowns: Catherine, and Margaret, riding every wave of every name this life has carried since Antioch. It is the same voice that once prayed inside a dragon's belly, that leapt from a housetop at fifteen, that fled a wedding bed at midnight, that raised another woman's child in silence for ten years without complaint, arriving now in Lorraine to counsel a shepherd girl who will, within five years, be asked to make exactly the same kind of leap.

stops.name: Lyon, Gerson's De Mirabili Victoria
stops.campa: In his cell at the Celestine convent in Lyon, old and in exile, the theologian Jean Gerson finishes a short defense of the Maid a month after Orléans is relieved: De Mirabili Victoria, on the miraculous victory, citing the precedent of Thecla, Pelagia, and Marina as church mothers who dressed as men, faced the devil directly, and answered to no authority but God's own voice. He will be dead within two months. It is the first time in this book the timelines are named together in a single sentence by someone outside the family of their own legend, in defense of a fourth woman entirely.

stops.name: Embrun, Gelu's dissertation on the Maid
stops.campa: In the mountain seat of Embrun, Archbishop Jacques Gelu writes his own dissertation on the Maid of Orléans, De Puella Aurelianensi, reaching for the same three names Gerson reached for in Lyon: Thecla, Pelagia, Marina, to argue that a woman's authority, when it comes directly from God, need not apologize for the clothes it wears to do God's work. Two churchmen in two cities, writing within weeks of each other without conferring, arrive at the same short list of precedents, as if the runaway brides of the fourth and fifth centuries had been waiting fourteen hundred years for a case exactly like this one.

stops.name: Beaurevoir, the leap relived
stops.campa: At Beaurevoir, against Catherine's daily counsel but not, the trial will insist later, against Margaret's own oldest example, Jehanne climbs to the tower window and leaps sixty feet to the ground rather than be handed to the English and see Compiègne burned. She is found unbroken, senseless, unbleeding: Pelagia's fifteen-year-old leap from an Antioch housetop relived eleven centuries later by a girl who has never read the Golden Legend but carries its logic anyway: some doors are better gone through at a fall than opened. Article 65 of the accusation will call it despair. This family has another word for it.
stops.quote: I did it not out of despair, but in the hope of saving my body and of going to succour the good people in need.
stops.quote_source: Trial of condemnation, session of 14 March 1431 (shared pin, see joan_of_arc.journey.json)
